transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-12 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (CTO), Jenna (Infra), Luis (SRE)

Summary: Deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for StratusAI's inference workloads. Covered burst policies, queueing behavior, reserved GPU sizing, KV cache hit patterns, batching and quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a small benchmark and share pricing examples for reserved capacity.

Topics: autoscaling policies, burst capacity, queueing models, reserved GPUs, kv cache warmup, batching windows, quantization impact, VPC private control plane, SLA targets

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Reed: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood, i'll run the intro. uh, priya on the demo side, and with stratus we have mark, jenna, luis. can you confirm audio?
[00:12] Mark Liu: yeah loud and clear, thanks. our main ask today is to understand how you think about autoscaling when we have spiky traffic — think bursty inference for search and a real-time assistant.
[00:24] Priya Shah: great, thanks. quick agenda: a) how autoscale + reserved capacity interplay, b) queueing and burst policies, c) kv cache and batching effects on capacity, d) quantization and perf trade-offs, e) open q's around VPC/on-prem. sound good?
[00:38] Jenna Park: yep that's perfect. just so you know we have a p95 latency target of 120ms for search completions and for assistant flows p95 is 400ms but we care about tail. daily tokens ~45M, but bursts up to 6x baseline for short windows.
[00:53] Luis Gomez: and we have strict data residency; private deployment might be necessary depending on SOC2 details.
[01:02] Alex Reed: cool, so first the high-level. our recommended pattern is reserved capacity sized for steady-state with autoscale + burst pool for short spikes. reserved GPUs handle baseline throughput and the burst pool gives you headroom  — bursts can be on the same pool or a cheaper lower-priority pool depending on SLA.
[01:22] Priya Shah: to add, we use a queuing model in the router: incoming requests either hit an available worker immediately or queue up with a bounded queue. queueing behavior depends on policy — you can set latency SLO vs cost thresholds; e.g., short queue with aggressive autoscale vs long queue and lower cost.
[01:41] Mark Liu: can you explain how KV cache impacts both latency and reserved capacity? we plan to cache conversation prefixes for the assistant.
[01:50] Priya Shah: yes. KV cache dramatically reduces per-token compute once warm — that means higher effective throughput per GPU for ongoing sessions. but it requires sticky routing to maintain hot KV in local memory. so reserved capacity with sticky routing keeps hot keys on the same worker, which reduces bursty cold starts. if you rely on stateless routing you lose cache gains and need more GPUs.
[02:12] Jenna Park: sticky routing, gotcha. what's the warmup time and memory cost?
[02:18] Priya Shah: warmup depends on model size and typical session length; for a 7B-ish model warmup could be a few hundred tokens; for 70B it's more. memory: KV entries are roughly proportional to seq len * num sessions; we can surface estimates in the bench.
[02:33] Alex Reed: note also our continuous batching strategy — we open a micro-batching window (e.g., 10-20ms) to combine reqs for better GPU throughput. batching increases throughput but can add queuing delay. so there's a trade between token cost and latency.
[02:50] Luis Gomez: what's the impact of quantization on latency and on reserved GPU sizing? we plan to use int8 quant to save cost if possible.
[02:58] Priya Shah: quantization lowers memory and can improve throughput on certain kernels, but it depends on model architecture and hardware (some GPUs have better int8 perf). int8 often reduces memory footprint so you can fit more KV or bigger batch sizes per GPU, lowering reserved GPU count. however, quant can introduce slight quality regressions; teams typically run evals on their prompts first.
[03:18] Mark Liu: queueing model — when you have bursts 6x, do you recommend keeping queues short and spinning up more burst GPUs quickly, or letting queue grow for a few seconds while maintaining cheaper baseline?
[03:29] Priya Shah: depends on your user experience. For interactive assistant flows with 400ms p95 target you want aggressive autoscale and short queues. For search rank jobs where latency can be a bit higher, you can allow longer queues and save cost. We typically recommend a hybrid: reserved capacity sized for p95 under baseline, a burst pool with pre-warmed instances (fast scale) for immediate headroom, and a cold pool that can take minutes to spin up for prolonged high traffic.
[03:56] Jenna Park: how do pre-warmed instances work with VPC/private deployments? any networking constraints that slow warmup?
[04:05] Alex Reed: in Private mode we offer a private control plane and agents that run in your VPC. Pre-warmed GPUs are managed by your cluster so warmup time can be shorter because they're local; but bootstrap still depends on image pull, model load times, and KMS access for keys. if you have on-prem air-gapped setups, you can keep images and models locally to minimize that.
[04:28] Luis Gomez: okay — can you share typical numbers: e.g., how many concurrent requests per A100 p4/8 for 13B vs 70B model with kv cache hit rate of 60%?
[04:38] Priya Shah: rough order: with KV cache 60% hit, a 13B model on A100 might handle ~150-250 concurrent small requests (short seqs) with batching; 70B maybe 30-60 depending on batch. without cache those numbers drop a lot. we'll run a short synthetic bench to get closer numbers for your exact prompt distribution.
[05:00] Mark Liu: we need guidance for reserved commit: if we sign up for 4 reserved GPU slots, what's the expected p95 across our two endpoints?
[05:09] Priya Shah: we'll map your token volumes and p95 targets to GPU throughput with the bench results. but as a rule of thumb, reserved capacity should cover steady-state QPS under expected cache hit rates; autoscaling covers short spikes.
[05:21] Alex Reed: also there's a policy you can set: "burst-on-reserved" which allows reserved GPUs to temporarily exceed baseline limits at higher cost, vs "burst-on-shared" which pulls from a shared burst pool. both have tradeoffs for predictability.
[05:37] Jenna Park: what's the billing model for burst? is it per-minute or per-second?
[05:43] Alex Reed: hosted billing is per-second with minute-level rounding; reserved capacity is monthly commit with overage billed per-second. For Dedicated, burst pools can be configured as on-demand pools with different pricing tiers. we'll send examples in the pricing sheet.
[05:57] Luis Gomez: question about queueing: what happens to requests that time out in the queue? do you return partials or immediate errors?
[06:04] Priya Shah: you can configure timeouts and partial response policies. for streaming workloads we can return partial tokens and continue processing; for strict whole-response APIs we typically return an error once timeout hits. We also support retry policies and automatic fallback to smaller models for lower-latency failures.
[06:21] Mark Liu: fallback to smaller models — is that automated? can we define rules?
[06:27] Alex Reed: yes policy-driven. you can configure fallbacks (e.g., route to 7B quantized variant if 70B latency exceeds threshold), or region fallback if a zone has capacity issues. The router supports model families mapping.
[06:39] Jenna Park: any recommended autoscale config for our burst patterns (6x for 1-2 min windows, daily peak at 11am for 30m)?
[06:48] Priya Shah: recommendation: reserved GPUs sized for baseline + 20%; pre-warmed burst pool equal to ~30-40% of baseline for sub-minute bursts; autoscale ramp that can add additional nodes for sustained >5min spikes. Use sticky routing for sessions to retain KV cache. Also set micro-batch window to 10ms for low latency assistant flows, maybe 20ms for search to improve cost.
[07:13] Luis Gomez: how do we monitor and decide when to convert burst to reserved? we want to avoid over-committing.
[07:20] Alex Reed: Redwood Console provides cost/latency dashboards; you can set alerts on sustained usage and we'll show recommended commit tiers based on trailing 7/30/90-day usage. There's also an "autosuggest" that flags workloads that would benefit from more reserved.
[07:36] Mark Liu: about KV cache eviction — if cache evicts under pressure during a burst, does that spike latency retroactively?
[07:43] Priya Shah: yes evictions cause more cold kv hits which increase compute per-request; we recommend monitoring cache hit rate and provisioning memory headroom for expected concurrent sessions. For large session counts you either increase reserved GPU memory or lower per-session seq length via truncation.
[08:00] Jenna Park: security question: does reserved GPU memory ever store customer data outside encrypted mem? and how do you handle KMS access in private?
[08:09] Alex Reed: we never persist customer data in host storage unless configured. KV cache resides in memory, encrypted in transit; for Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM and we never send plaintext keys to our control plane. We'll share SOC2 docs and architecture notes.
[08:27] Mark Liu: ok great. let's talk about a proposed test — you mentioned a synthetic bench. what should that look like?
[08:33] Priya Shah: 50k tokens over a mix of short (20-50 tok) assistant sessions and medium search queries with simulated 6x spikes. Run with kv-cache on and off, quantized and fp16 variants, and with batching windows 10ms/20ms. We'll output p50/p95/p99 latencies, throughput, cache hit rates, and GPU utilization.
[08:53] Luis Gomez: that sounds good — one more: how do cloud region routing and cross-region fallbacks affect latency?
[08:59] Alex Reed: cross-region fallbacks have network RTT costs; for latency-sensitive apps keep traffic in-region and use multi-AZ within region with local fallbacks. We can route by geo and tenant.
[09:11] Jenna Park: are there any gotchas for our k8s infra? we run EKS with node pools and custom scheduling.
[09:18] Priya Shah: for k8s we recommend GPU node pools dedicated to inference with taints/tolerations and pod priority classes. Pre-pull images and use warm pool nodes to minimize cold start. Also use our sidecar metrics exporter to feed console dashboards.
[09:33] Mark Liu: ok, let's recap next steps.
[09:36] Alex Reed: recap — alex will send pricing and reserved examples; priya will run the synthetic bench and share results; jenna will send token volumes and p95 numbers; we schedule a follow-up in two weeks to review bench and commit guidance.
[09:52] Jenna Park: thanks all, this was super helpful.
[09:56] Luis Gomez: thanks.
[09:58] Alex Reed: thanks everyone — we'll follow up.

End transcript. Note: transcription contains some minor noise ("kv cash" sometimes) and occasional mis-attribution.
